01

The idea

Wealth management interfaces are built for compliance. PRISM asks what one built for trust would look like instead.

The starting point was a client UX role brief. Rather than submit a mood board response, I treated it as a real product problem: advisors and clients in wealth management are asked to trust increasingly automated, data-heavy tools, but most interfaces in this space still read like a spreadsheet with a login screen.

PRISM became case study eight in my portfolio: a self-initiated concept for a connected wealth intelligence platform that turns portfolio data, market intelligence, and client actions into a single governed workflow, for both the advisor workspace and the client-facing portal.

The honest brief I set myself was to address the domain gap directly rather than assume it away. Financial services interfaces carry real consequences, an AI suggestion that looks autonomous, a chart with no source, an action with no audit trail, all of those are trust failures before they are visual ones. So the project isn't just a UI exercise, it's a test of whether I can hold product logic, responsible AI thinking, and design system discipline together across a full product surface.

02

Brand identity

A prism refracts one source of light into clarity. That is the whole brand in one image.

The mark is a low-poly triangular prism built on true equilateral geometry, symmetrical and precise. It reads as a data structure as easily as an optical object, which matters for a product whose entire value proposition is turning complex financial information into something a client can actually understand.

03

Product thinking and UX architecture

The hardest design problem was not the UI. It was how to show AI-assisted advice without implying the AI decides.

Every AI-assisted view in PRISM follows the same disclosed chain: evidence first, confidence stated honestly, limitations named, a human review step before anything moves, then an action, then a permanent audit trail. Nowhere does the product suggest the system executes a financial decision on its own.

  • Evidence. The data behind any suggestion is shown, not hidden behind a confident summary.
  • Confidence. Stated plainly rather than implied through tone or certainty of language.
  • Limitations. Named directly, what the model does not know or cannot account for.
  • Human review. A required step before any suggestion becomes an action.
  • Decision and action. Made by the advisor or client, never by the system alone.
  • Audit trail. Every action is permanently logged.

Two surfaces, one system

Advisor workspace: portfolio oversight, market intelligence, AI-assisted review queues, and client management, built for someone managing many relationships at once, so density and scannability matter more than delight.

Client portal: the same underlying data, translated into a calmer, more narrative view: performance, actions awaiting the client's own approval, and a plain-language explanation of what the advisor and the AI assistant actually did.

Every number in the prototype is simulated. Where that matters for credibility, financial figures, portfolio values, market data, the interface and the accompanying documentation say so plainly. A prototype can prove the design is coherent; it cannot and does not claim to prove compliance, security, or production readiness. That distinction was a deliberate design decision, not a disclaimer bolted on afterward.

04

UI design

Deep navy foundation, one disciplined accent blue, data given room to breathe.

The UI leans on the brand's near-black navy as a base, reserving colour for what actually needs attention: the accent blue for primary actions, status colours for portfolio and market states, and a dedicated numeric type style for anything that is a figure a client might act on.

Financial data gets its own type scale. Portfolio values, percentage changes, and tickers use a dedicated monospace numeric scale, so figures stay legible and comparable at a glance, the same reason trading interfaces default to monospace for numbers.

Status is colour-coded, sparingly. Success, warning, info, error, pending, and review each carry a defined status colour, used only on the specific element that needs it, never as a background wash. Colour is a signal in PRISM, not a decoration.

05

Design system and component governance

Primitives, then semantic tokens, then components. One source of truth, not thirty different copies of a button.

This is the part of PRISM I would put in front of a senior product design panel first. The file is not just screens, it is a governed system: primitive colour, spacing, radius, and sizing tokens, semantic tokens built on top of them, and a component library of ten governed sets built as master component to variant to instance, not independent frame copies.

A real audit, not a tidy-up

01

Audit

Checked the file's own governance panel, variable collections, text styles, and component sets, against what was actually bound versus hardcoded.

02

Diagnose

Found three different "brand blues" live across the token collection, the master button component, and the product screens, none of them matched the actual approved brand asset.

03

Fix

Sampled the true colour values from the approved logo asset, recalibrated the root primitives, then bound the button component's states to the semantic tokens instead of a hardcoded hex.

04

Verify

Migrated 21 independent-frame CTA buttons to real component instances, piloted one, confirmed position, label, and click-through interaction survived, then scaled to the rest.

05

Document

Logged what was fixed, what was deliberately left alone, a missing secondary button variant, an unmapped brand colour, and why, rather than silently overwriting a system I had not fully understood yet.

06

Product build and prototype

Real interactions, not the appearance of them.

Every primary action in the investor demo flow is a genuine Figma prototype connection, click triggers, real navigation, not static frames dressed up to look clickable. The demo runs as a ten-screen guided path: sign-in, portfolio overview, client book, markets, AI-assisted review, human sign-off, and a client-facing summary, with a restart loop back to the start for repeat walkthroughs.

Built for two audiences at once. One curated page in the file, the investor read-me, exists purely as a non-overlapping handoff surface: the finished product, its core journeys, and the design system, without exposing working history. The full working file, iteration history and all, is preserved separately rather than deleted, so the process stays honest without cluttering the presentation.

A React build, not just Figma. Alongside the Figma system, PRISM exists as a deployable React app, Vite, Tailwind, React Router, covering the client portal and advisor workspace, so the design system had to hold up under real implementation constraints, not just look right in a static frame.

"For investors, start with the prototype flow. For design and engineering, use the read-me page as the curated handoff surface. Working history remains preserved in Archive and Source."Source: PRISM file read-me, written for the file itself
07

What this demonstrates

PRISM is as much a case study in design operations as it is in interface design.

  • Fintech and wealth-management UX judgement. Dense financial data made legible without losing precision, and a responsible AI interaction model that never lets an assistant appear to act alone on someone's money.
  • Design system discipline under real conditions. Not a clean system built once, but one audited, found imperfect, and corrected in the open, primitives recalibrated against a real brand asset, components migrated from independent copies to governed instances, gaps documented rather than papered over.
  • Investor and stakeholder communication. A file built to be handed to product designers, engineers, and investors alike, each with their own entry point, without needing a verbal walkthrough to make sense of it.
  • Honesty about its own limits. This is a design artefact. It proves the product is coherent, considered, and implementation-ready in intent. It does not claim to prove security, compliance, or regulatory approval, because a Figma file never can.
